tip: The ending -la/-le means with: 'arkadaşımla' = with my colleague, from 'arkadaşım' plus -la.
-abil- adds can, and as a question it becomes a polite request: 'açabilir misiniz' = could you open.
-dığında means when something happens, attached to the verb: 'yapıldığında' = when it is made.
The -erdi/-ardı ending is the used-to past: 'çizerdi' = used to draw regularly.
Unreal wish: -sa on the condition, -irdim on the result. 'olsa' ... 'alırdım' = if I had ... I would buy.
-maktadır is a formal written present continuous, common in news: 'yapmaktadır' = is making.
Comparisons add -den to the thing compared plus 'daha' (more): 'kardeşinden daha uzun' = taller than the brother.
-dığım turns a verb into the thing that I did, set before a noun: 'gördüğüm manzara' = the view that I saw.
The -da ending can mean per for frequency: 'haftada üç kez' = three times a week.
Add -dır to a time span to mean for that long: 'yüzyıllardır' = for centuries and still going.
-ip chains two verbs with one subject, and only the last carries tense: 'bulup getirdi' = found and brought.
-an turns a verb into the one who does it, set before a noun: 'spor yapan' = who exercise.
Past what-if: -seydi on the condition, -mazdı on the result. 'erimeseydi' ... 'daralmazdı' = if it hadn't melted, wouldn't have shrunk.
'büyümektedir' uses -mektedir, a formal written present continuous seen in news and reports. Everyday speech would just say 'büyüyor'.
'beş yıldır' keeps the present tense 'yaşıyoruz' where English switches to have been living. The -dir on a time span means for that long.
'etmezseniz' stacks the negative -mez onto the if-ending -se: if you do not pay attention. The positive, 'ederseniz', means if you do.
'başlar' and 'biter' use the -r ending for timeless, habitual facts like a school calendar, not one event happening right now.
'dikkat etmek' takes the -a ending: 'çocuklara dikkat et' (watch the children) uses -a, not the plain object form 'çocukları'.
'kurtulmak' pairs with the -ten ending: 'trafikten kurtuluruz' (we get free from traffic) marks what you escape from.
'etme' is the singular do not: 'acele etme' to one person. For plural or polite address you would say 'etmeyin' instead.
-ken means while or as: 'giderken' is as you leave, pinning one action to the moment of another.
'uyuyamıyorum' carries -ama, cannot: I am unable to sleep. Without it, 'uyumuyorum' would just mean I am not sleeping.
'bir türlü' with a negative verb means no matter what, never: 'bir türlü bitiremez' = she can never finish it.
'söylerdi' is the -r form plus -di, the used-to past for a repeated habit, not one single occasion of singing.
'olmuş' uses -miş, reporting something inferred or heard rather than personally witnessed: it has apparently become popular.
'doldurun' and 'bırakın' take -un/-ın, the polite or plural command. To one person informally it is 'doldur' and 'bırak'.
'tehlikeliymiş' adds -ymiş to an adjective to report hearsay about the past: it was apparently dangerous, so I was told.
'kışın' means in winter, a set time adverb built from 'kış'. Summer works the same way: 'yazın'.
'artacakmış' blends the future -acak with reported -mış: prices will reportedly rise, a prediction you heard rather than know firsthand.
'oynayarak' uses -arak, by doing: it tells you how they had fun, by playing snowball.
